q-115261.ma_answer_value: $f(x)$ is concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}$

evidence.quote: Therefore, the function must be concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}.$
evidence.method: Independently matched the saved worked-solution conclusion to the original state.json before-layout choices; neither submitted answers nor prior repair drafts were used.

repairs.old: Given that the tangent line approximation to the function $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2},$ which of the following must be true?
repairs.new: Given that the tangent line approximation to a differentiable function $f(x)$ at every point in an open interval containing $x=\sqrt{2}$ strictly overestimates the values of the function at every other point in that interval, which of the following must be true?
repairs.reason: Replace the invalid one-base-point converse by the tangent characterization of concavity on an interval; strict overestimation excludes the linear distractor.

repairs.old:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function, we have

$$
L(x)>f(x),
$$

that is, the line $L(x)$ must be above the graph of $f(x)$ near the point  $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the function must be concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}.$
repairs.new:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at every point $a$ in the given neighborhood strictly overestimates the values of the function at every other point, we have

$$
L_a(x)>f(x)\quad (x\ne a),
$$

that is, each tangent line $L_a(x)$ lies above the graph of $f(x)$ throughout the neighborhood, with equality only at $x=a.$ A differentiable function whose graph lies below each of its tangent lines on an interval is concave down on that interval.

Therefore, the function must be concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}.$
repairs.reason: Apply the tangent criterion at all base points and explicitly allow equality at the point of tangency.

validation.mathematics: For any a<b in the neighborhood, the two strict tangent inequalities give f′(b)<(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)<f′(a). Thus f′ is strictly decreasing and f is concave down. Strict concavity excludes a local or global minimum at the interior point, concave-up behavior, and linearity.

q-115261.discussion: Retains the MA intended conclusion and all five choices. Strengthening the scope of the tangent hypothesis is sufficient; no new assumptions about a nonzero or continuous second derivative are needed. One tangent at one point would not establish this conclusion.

repairs.old: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
repairs.new: Which of the following expressions is obtained by using the pointwise polar arc-length integrand for ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2<\theta<\pi /2$? Interpret the endpoint integrals as improper integrals.
repairs.reason: Exclude the undefined endpoints, explicitly interpret the integrals improperly, and test the pointwise arc-length formula rather than equality of divergent integral values.

repairs.old:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$
repairs.new:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

These endpoint integrals are improper and diverge to $+\infty.$ The requested expression is determined by the pointwise arc-length integrand on $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2.$
repairs.reason: Correct the isolated upper-limit typo and explain both the infinite length and the pointwise criterion that selects the intended expression.

validation.mathematics: On (-pi/2,pi/2), sec(theta)>0, r′=3 sec^3(theta) tan(theta), and sqrt(r^2+(r′)^2)=sec^3(theta) sqrt(1+9 tan^2(theta)). Only option 4 has this pointwise integrand with the correct parameter interval. Option 1 has the same divergent value but the wrong integrand (at theta=0 its integrand is 3 instead of 1); options 0, 2, and 3 have the wrong interval. The endpoint integrals diverge because the speed is at least sec^3(theta).

q-123439.discussion: The original equivalent-value question remains ambiguous even after merely declaring improper integrals, because more than one option is +infinity. Explicitly asking for the pointwise arc-length construction resolves that ambiguity and preserves every option and every intended endpoint. A finite replacement interval would force collateral edits to otherwise useful choices and has no source-supported preferred value.

repairs.old:
Which of the following augmented matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
repairs.new:
Which of the following augmented matrices have coefficient matrices that are **not** in row echelon form? Treat the final column of each augmented matrix as its constants column.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
repairs.reason: Ask explicitly about coefficient matrices, which is the object the saved MA solution actually classifies; identify the omitted constants column.

repairs.old:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since ${b}_{22}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ is **not** in row echelon form.
repairs.new:
A coefficient matrix, obtained by omitting the final column of its augmented matrix, is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The coefficient matrix of $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The coefficient matrix of $B$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entries of its first two rows are in columns $3$ and $2,$ respectively (condition II is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

- The coefficient matrix of $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ has a coefficient matrix that is **not** in row echelon form.
repairs.reason: Remove the false claim that augmented-matrix echelon form is defined by the coefficient matrix, consistently name the coefficient matrices, and identify B’s actual pivot-order violation.

validation.mathematics: Deleting the final columns leaves A with leading columns 1 and 2 followed by two zero rows; B with leading columns 3, 2, 1; and C with leading columns 1, 2, 5. Only B’s coefficient matrix fails row echelon form.

q-72575.discussion: Preserves the MA intended B-only key and every matrix entry. The repaired question uses the standard definition of row echelon form on the explicitly requested coefficient matrices; it does not redefine row echelon form for augmented matrices.

repairs.new: Calculate the $x$-intercepts of the real locus ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x+6y+12=0$
repairs.reason: Stop asserting that the equation defines a real circle; its real locus is a well-defined empty set.

repairs.old:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts.  

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x+6y+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2x+6\cdot 0+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1+12 & =0+1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+12 & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $x,$ there is no $x$ such that $(x-1)^{2}=-11.$ Therefore, circle has no $x$-intercepts, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13959190/assets/ea1410ea792ac5fb09316bc6d417c2ba46f84c050491b1e351f360eac50deb6c.png)
repairs.new:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts.  

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the locus and solve the resulting equation for $x,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x+6y+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2x+6\cdot 0+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1+12 & =0+1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+12 & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $x,$ there is no $x$ such that $(x-1)^{2}=-11.$ Therefore, the locus has no $x$-intercepts.

repairs.reason: Delete the extra rate-of-growth layer so the stated proportionality is D′=kt, matching the requested first-order model and the MA choice.

repairs.old:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The rate of growth of a **car's displacement** $D(t)$ **increases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the **time** $t$ since the car started moving.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *car's displacement* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *interval of time* since the car started moving. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}∝t.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the car's displacement *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=kt.
$$

repairs.old: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
repairs.new: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find unit vectors along the principal axes of the quadratic form.
repairs.reason: Ask for the principal-axis directions of the well-defined quadratic form, preserving the given matrix and eigenvalues while removing the impossible level set.

repairs.old:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

validation.mathematics: A(1,1)^T=0 and A(-1,1)^T=-4(-1,1)^T. After division by sqrt(2), these vectors have unit norm and zero dot product, yielding Q^T A Q=diag(0,-4). The two eigenspaces are the lines x2=x1 and x2=-x1. None of options 1–4 has both vectors on those lines, so only option 0 is an eigenbasis. The original level x^T A x=7 is empty because x^T A x=-2(x1-x2)^2<=0.
